extracted.intended_audience: attorneys registered to practice before the USPTO; regulators and disciplinary counsel; legal practitioners interested in professional-conduct and reciprocal-discipline rules
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and imposition of reciprocal discipline by the USPTO Director under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 based on a state's disciplinary action, including the §11.24(f) requirements for imposing a nunc pro tunc suspension and related procedural obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 / violation of 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(h)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspension from practice before the USPTO may be imposed for violation of 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(h) when the attorney "[is] suspended on ethical grounds by a duly constituted authority of a State."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO Director can impose discipline identical to the state's discipline unless the respondent establishes by clear and convincing evidence that imposition of identical discipline would be unwarranted. The final order here suspends Respondent nunc pro tunc for the same thirty-day period as the Indiana suspension (June 14, 2017–July 13, 2017).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(f) requirements for nunc pro tunc reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.24(f) criteria include prompt notification to the OED Director of the state suspension, voluntary cessation of all activities related to practice before the Office, and compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED Director agreed Respondent satisfied 11.24(f) because: (a) Respondent promptly notified the OED Director of his suspension; (b) Respondent established by clear and convincing evidence that he voluntarily ceased all activities related to practice before the Office; and (c) Respondent complied with all provisions of 37 C.F.R. § 11.58. Satisfaction of these elements supports imposition of the state discipline nunc pro tunc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence (Indiana disciplinary proceedings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission carries the burden of proof to demonstrate attorney misconduct by clear and convincing evidence (Ind. Admission and Discipline Rule 23(14)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court reviews the whole record de novo but gives emphasis to hearing officer findings due to direct observation of witnesses; conflicting evidence may be resolved in favor of the credited testimony if Commission fails to meet its burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review: de novo review with emphasis on hearing officer findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indiana Supreme Court reviews de novo all matters presented, including the hearing officer's report and the entire record, but gives emphasis to the hearing officer's findings because of their opportunity to observe witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although hearing officer findings receive emphasis, the Court reserves the ultimate determination and may reweigh evidence where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.4(a)(1) and 1.4(a)(5) — consultation/communication about limited scope of representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules 1.4(a)(1) and 1.4(a)(5) concern informing clients about the scope of representation; the hearing officer found no violation here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court noted that the written agreements did not fully spell out division of labor but that the Rules do not require such matters to be in writing; credited Respondent's testimony that he discussed the division of labor during the initial phone call and made himself available — the Commission did not call clients to rebut that testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.5(e) — fee splitting between lawyers not in the same firm
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 1.5(e) sets forth three requirements that must be met for a division of a fee between lawyers who are 'not in the same firm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If those formal requirements (e.g., client agreement in writing specifying the share each lawyer will receive) are not met, a division violates Rule 1.5(e). The Court analyzed 'same firm' status using factors such as contractual terms, how tasks were allocated between entities, whether the local attorney maintained a separate firm, use of firm letterhead, and the economic relationship (fixed small sums vs. full client fee). On balance the Court found Respondent was not in the same firm as CAS and therefore violated Rule 1.5(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.5(a) — charging an unreasonable fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 1.5(a) prohibits charging or assisting in charging an unreasonable fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonrefundable retainers generally are permissible only to the extent they reserve the attorney's time and availability. Here, CAS charged ~ $1,200 nonrefundable retainers while local counsel was paid only $75 for minimal services and clients were charged recurring monthly fees not tied to work performed; the Court found Respondent assisted CAS in charging an unreasonable fee (violations of Rules 8.4(a) and 1.5(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 5.3(b) — supervision of nonlawyers
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawyer with 'direct supervisory authority' over a nonlawyer must make reasonable efforts to ensure the nonlawyer's conduct is compatible with the lawyer's professional responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hearing officer credited Respondent's testimony that CAS paralegals were supervised by an Indiana-licensed attorney on CAS's central staff and found no violation; the Court deferred to that credibility determination where the Commission failed to meet its burden to the contrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 7.5(a)(4) — use of trade name
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 7.5(a)(4) imposes requirements upon an attorney's use of a trade name, including that 'the name shall include the name of a lawyer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court found no violation because CAS's website and agreements listed 'McCann Law Group' and Respondent generally used his own firm name and letterhead in pleadings and correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 5.5(a) — assisting in the unauthorized practice of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 5.5(a) prohibits assisting nonlawyers or entities in the unauthorized practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court considers business-model factors: marginalization of attorney role by central staff, low fixed payments to local counsel, allocation of most tasks to out-of-state staff, fees not tethered to services rendered, and lack of client disclosure about fee allocation. If attorney involvement is necessary for the company to provide services, and the model marginalizes substantial attorney involvement, participation constitutes assisting the unauthorized practice of law. The Court found Respondent violated Rule 5.5(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8.4(c) — dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 8.4(c) proscribes conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding under 8.4(c) requires evidence of dishonest or deceitful intent. The Court declined to find a violation here because the record did not establish Respondent acted with intent to deceive or to generate quick fees at clients' expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8.4(d) — conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 8.4(d) concerns conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court requires evidence of specific prejudice or harm to support a Rule 8.4(d) violation; mere use of one's own letterhead or firm identification without proof of resulting prejudice is insufficient. The Court found no violation here due to lack of evidence of prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors and precedential comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court weighs aggravating and mitigating factors and compares prior cases (e.g., Dilk, Joyce, Fratini, Jackson) when deciding the appropriate discipline and whether automatic reinstatement is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant factors include extent of misconduct, prior disciplinary record, evidence of particularized client harm, whether the misconduct was pervasive in the attorney's practice, subjective intent (selfish motive vs. well-intentioned), mitigation (e.g., small part of practice devoted to referrals, lack of prior discipline, good faith), and precedent sanctions. These considerations supported a 30‑day suspension with automatic reinstatement here rather than a longer suspension without automatic reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic reinstatement and conditions for reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatic reinstatement after a suspension may follow if conditions are met and no other suspensions remain in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Indiana order provided for automatic reinstatement after the 30‑day suspension (subject to Admission and Discipline Rule 23(18)(a)), and the USPTO Final Order reinstated Respondent nunc pro tunc effective July 14, 2017. The Court contrasted cases where longer suspensions without automatic reinstatement were imposed when misconduct and harm were greater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural duties of a suspended attorney (Admission and Discipline Rule 23(26))
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended attorney shall not undertake any new legal matters between service of the opinion and the effective date of the suspension and must fulfill duties of a suspended attorney under the applicable rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Indiana Court ordered Respondent not to undertake new matters and to comply with duties while suspended; the USPTO order noted waiver of certain 37 C.F.R. sections and directed publication in the Official Gazette consistent with 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.24.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication requirement (Official Gazette / public disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director is ordered to publish a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the provided notice of suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary decisions are available for public review at the OED FOIA Reading Room; public notice summarizes the basis for suspension and the applicable rules violated.
